text: Chapter 10, the notification system. Let's see how it works in about three minutes.

The simplest design: a trigger service calls one notification server. It reads the database, renders the message, then calls Apple push, Google push, an SMS provider, and an email provider directly. Every day: ten million push notifications, five million emails, and one million text messages.

This design has three problems. If that one server dies, every notification stops: a single point of failure. The database, cache, and sending logic are tied together, so you can't scale them separately. And sending eats resources, which makes it a bottleneck.

The fix has four steps. Move the database and cache out of the server. Scale the notification servers out horizontally. Put message queues in the middle, one per channel. Finally, workers for each channel pull from their queue and call the third party.

So here is the whole pipeline. The trigger service calls the API. A notification server validates the request and fetches metadata, then puts the event on a queue. A worker picks it up, calls the third party, and the message reaches the user. The caller can leave as soon as the queue has it.

Queues also smooth out traffic spikes. More importantly, they isolate channels. If the SMS provider goes down, only the SMS queue backs up, while push and email keep flowing. But a queue doesn't add third-party capacity. If the backlog won't shrink, look at channel limits and worker throughput.

Reliability comes from two things. First, write each notification to a log database with its status, so it survives a crash. Second, when the third party fails, retry with growing delays. And an expired verification code shouldn't be sent at all.

Retries cause duplicates. The book's answer is to deduplicate by event ID. But check-then-send isn't enough: two workers can both see the event as new. You need an atomic claim plus a stable idempotency key. Aim for at-least-once delivery with deduplication, not a casual promise of exactly once.

Before sending, a few gates remain. First, check user settings: if they opted out of this type, don't send. Then rate limiting caps how often one user is notified. Finally, apply a template, so the format stays consistent.
Remember three things: queues, retry plus deduplication, and settings plus rate limits. And one more: the third party accepting a message doesn't mean the user has seen it.
